```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = FALSE, comment = "#>")
# Scoring with the CNNs needs the Python Keras backend and the models downloaded
# from Hugging Face. CRAN has neither, so that step only runs where NOT_CRAN is
# set, Keras 3.15.0 or later can be reached, and the download succeeds.
has_keras <- identical(Sys.getenv("NOT_CRAN"), "true") && isTRUE(tryCatch(
  numeric_version(keras3::keras$`__version__`) >= "3.15.0",
  error = function(e) FALSE
)) && !is.null(tryCatch(suppressMessages(AutoCDAScorer::download_models()), error = function(e) NULL))
```

This guide shows the three steps of scoring cell death areas (CDAs) with
AutoCDAScorer. First you load the CDA images. Then you check, with diagnostic
plots, that they resemble the images the models were trained on. Finally you
score them.

```{r setup}
library(AutoCDAScorer)
```

## Load the CDA images

There are two ways to load CDA images.

### From source images and bounding boxes

A source image shows several leaves, each with several infiltration sites. A
CSV file gives a bounding box around each CDA. You can make that file with
[CDALabeller](https://github.com/joshuandwilliams/CDALabeller), or with the
older CDAScorer. `crop_and_load_images()` crops each CDA from its source image.

The CSV needs the columns `img`, `x1`, `x2`, `y1` and `y2`. `img` is the path to
the source image. CDALabeller saves only the file name, so either run R from
the folder that holds the source images or add the folder first, as here:

```{r load_from_boxes}
example_dir <- system.file("extdata", "example_dataset", package = "AutoCDAScorer")
boxes <- read.csv(file.path(example_dir, "cdascorer_example.csv"))
boxes$img <- file.path(example_dir, "raw_images", boxes$img)
boxes_csv <- tempfile(fileext = ".csv")
write.csv(boxes, boxes_csv, row.names = FALSE)

# output_path saves a copy of each cropped CDA image
your_dataset <- crop_and_load_images(boxes_csv, output_path = file.path(tempdir(), "crops"))

show_test_image(your_dataset)
```

### From cropped CDA images

If your CDA images are already cropped, load them from their folder:

```{r load_cropped}
cropped_dir <- system.file("extdata", "example_dataset", "cropped_images", package = "AutoCDAScorer")
your_dataset <- load_images(cropped_dir)

show_test_image(your_dataset)
```

## Check the diagnostic plots

Models are only reliable on images like the ones they were trained on. The
diagnostic plots show how your CDA images compare with the training images.

The plots use principal component analysis (PCA). PCA reduces each image to a
few numbers, called principal components (PCs), that capture most of the
differences between images. Each small plot shows the training images (grey)
and your images on two PCs.

There are three plot types. `"convexhull"` draws the outline of the training
images. It colours your images blue if they fall inside it and red if not.
`"target"` draws concentric ellipses around the training images, and
`"density"` draws density contours.

Here is a sample of the training images themselves. They all fall inside the
outline, as they should:

```{r inside, fig.height = 5, fig.width = 6}
training_sample <- readRDS(file.path(example_dir, "training_subset", "good_dataset.rds"))
diagnostic_pca("ensemble", training_sample, num_pcs = 5, plot_type = "convexhull")
```

The same images with their colour channels swapped no longer resemble the
training images. Most fall outside the outline:

```{r outside, fig.height = 5, fig.width = 6}
swapped <- training_sample
swapped$images <- swapped$images[, , , c(3, 1, 2)]
diagnostic_pca("ensemble", swapped, num_pcs = 5, plot_type = "convexhull")
```

If most of your images fall outside the training images, do not rely on
AutoCDAScorer's scores for them. If only some do, try the plots for another
model. `"ordinal"` was trained on different images from `"ensemble"` and
`"geom_cnn"`, so its plot can differ.

Not every pair of PCs matters equally. The circles in the lower right show the
share of the differences between images that each pair of PCs explains. Each
circle matches the small plot in the mirror position across the diagonal. Give
more weight to the plots whose circles show larger percentages.

Here are all three plot types for the example CDA images:

```{r all_types, fig.height = 5, fig.width = 6}
diagnostic_pca("ensemble", your_dataset, num_pcs = 5, plot_type = "target", num_ellipses = 3)
diagnostic_pca("ensemble", your_dataset, num_pcs = 5, plot_type = "density", num_bins = 5)
diagnostic_pca("ensemble", your_dataset, num_pcs = 5, plot_type = "convexhull")
```

## Score the CDA images

Once a model's diagnostic plots look right for your images, score them with
that model. By default, `predict_score()` returns one cell death severity score
per image, from 0 (no cell death) to 6 (strong cell death). With
`softmax = TRUE`, it returns the probability of each score instead, with one
column per score.

```{r score, eval = has_keras}
your_scores <- predict_score("ensemble", your_dataset)
table(your_scores)
```

The `"ensemble"` and `"geom_cnn"` models use 16 convolutional neural networks
(CNNs). These need Python and Keras 3.15.0 or later, and the CNNs themselves,
which are downloaded from Hugging Face. Run each of these once:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
check_and_install_tensorflow()
download_models()
```

The `"ordinal"` model needs neither, and neither do the diagnostic plots.
